A.title: The Pyrrhic Condition
A.definition: Winning in a way that destroys what made winning worthwhile.
covers: Victories that cost what you were fighting to protect are systemic failures
Institutional incentive structures reward Pyrrhic outcomes
Diagnose by asking: what did winning cost?

B.title: Transfer Success
B.definition: A system preserves power by moving cost, risk, or blame onto weaker parties while keeping decision authority elsewhere.
covers: A recurring pattern where accountability travels downward but authority stays upward.
A designed outcome that looks like failure to the harmed party but success to the system.

A.title: Attrition by queue
A.definition: A filtering mechanism where queue structure, resets, and handoffs quietly remove people from service pathways.
covers: Multi-step waits with expiry windows, missed-call penalties, or restart requirements.
Neutral-seeming throughput controls that disproportionately expel people with less scheduling flexibility.

B.title: Delay as force
B.definition: A governance pattern where elapsed time is weaponized: delays exhaust options, reduce claims, and push people to withdraw or accept worse terms without an explicit denial.
covers: Wait times and review loops that increase burden for the claimant while preserving institutional flexibility.
Time costs shifted onto people with urgent needs, unstable income, or fragile health.
Waiting that raises the cost of refusal, relying on fatigue, deadlines, or uncertainty to force consent.

B.title: Temporal Capture

Waiting, paperwork, and procedural delay are temporal taxation

B.title: Coercive Waiting
B.definition: Time is used as pressure: delays exhaust options, narrow choices, and coerce agreement.
covers: A pattern where waiting increases the cost of refusal.
A tactic that relies on fatigue, deadlines, or uncertainty to force consent.

A.title: Credibility as Access Control
A.definition: Credibility is gatekeeping disguised as quality control. Who gets believed determines access.
covers: Credibility assessments function as structural filters
The credibility frame obscures power dynamics of who gets believed
Access to resources and justice depends on passing credibility gates

B.title: Reputation Membrane
B.definition: Safety or ethics language forms a protective membrane that shields reputations without creating real reversibility or repair.
covers: A focus on appearances of care over measurable remedy.
A system that treats transparency as optional while requiring positive messaging.

A.title: Refusability Gap
A.definition: The ability to say no is treated as optional when it should be a structural design requirement.
covers: Refusal is not currently designed into most systems
The absence of refusal points is a political choice
Systems that make refusal impossible are coercive by design

B.title: Coercion by Design
B.definition: Coercion is not accidental. It is designed into systems, and therefore can be designed out.
covers: Coercive outcomes result from design choices
Systems can be built where coercion is structurally impossible
Designers should bear the burden of proving non-coercion

A.title: Compliance Trap
A.definition: Warmth and niceness are used to secure compliance, making refusal feel like cruelty or betrayal.
covers: A social setup where refusal is framed as harm while compliance is framed as kindness.
A situation where relational tone is used to bypass consent.

covers: A reliance on paperwork or policy to replace moral judgment.
